THE SALARY, ALLOWANCES AND PENSION OF MEMBERS OF 
PARLIAMENT (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2006 
THE MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND THE 
MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI):   Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill further to amend the Salary, Allowances and Pension 
of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, as  passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration." 
Sir, this Bill is due to the compulsion of five-year term extension of 
the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Bill, which we 
passed earlier in 2001. Sir, as you know, the Salary, Allowances and Pension 
of Members of Parliament Bill is gove rned by article 106 of the Constitution. 
And, article 106 left this power to pe Parliament. The Parliament, accordingly, 
composed Joint Committee of Members of both the House to examine the 
whole aspect and to recommend to the House and the Cabinet as to what 
should be the allowances and salaries of the MPs, from time to time. Sir, in the 
recent times, there was lot of debate in  the media and many other areas as to 
whether MPs are taking more advantage and rest of the nation does not like it. 
That kind of a perception has been built. When MPs' issue regarding salaries, 
allowances, etc., comes, it appears to become the most juicy and choosy item 
for the media, especially the electronic  media. But, the reality is altogether 
different. I first thank the Joint Committee, which worked so hard calculating all 
the details of world Parliaments, and I c an say, Sir, indian MPs represent the 
highest number of 
304 

[24 August, 2006]                        RAJYA SABHA 
population in the world in a particular segment of Lok Sabha, and accordingly, 
those, who are in the Rajya Sabha, also  represent State Assemblies by their 
support. And, therefore, I te ll you, Sir, that MPs of India still rank lowest paid 
in comparsion with the MPs of the developed nations of the world 
democracies. It is the position still today, Sir, with all facts and figures. 
Unfortunately, a section of Indian media, the electronic media, never projected 
and placed it. 
Sir, in 1971, when I became a Member of Lok Sabha for the first 
time, I remember I went to the Unit ed Kingdom as part of Commonwealth 
delegation. The British Member of Pa rliament in the House of Commons 
asked me a few questions. Do you have office in your constituency? I said, 
'no'. Do you have office in Delhi? I sa id, 'no'. Do you have a transport to tour? 
I said, 'no'. Do you have a Personal Secretary? I said, 'no'. He asked, how do 
you function? I said, we go to the people, come back, collect their papers, 
and, write to the Minister. He safd, it is very absurd. It was in 1971. I 
remember, there was a stenographic pool here and I had to wait in queues for 
hours together to get one letter typed. Those days are gone. In 2001, rightly 
my predecessor, Pramod Mahajanji, br ought the legislation based on the 
recommendations of the Joint Committee of Parliament on the Consumer 
Price Index, and, from Rs. 4,000, the sa lary was increased to Rs. 12,000. He 
gave that logic of the day which was absolutely correct. Sir, why did I come 
forward today? Sir, the existing salary and allowances are effective up to 14 th 
September, 2006. The proble m is that if it is not passed before that and it 
expires at 12' O clock in the night on 14 th September, then we go back to Rs. 
4,000/-. 
Last time, the Government said that it would be for a period of five 
years and after five years, Parliament would review and come back with the 
proposal and then the Government would consider. 
Accordingly, the Committee gave this suggestion and the 
recommendation. I took it to the Cabi net. The Cabinet considered the whole 
aspect, not fully. My dear friend, Mr.  Chidambaram, did not agree to all the 
recommendations but substantial part was accepted, and, I was duty bound to 
come before both the Houses and explain it. Therefore, Sir, I would like to 
submit that I thank all the Members wh o have worked hard. Sir, nobody just 
tries to understand the condition of an  MP of India. All these perks and 
facilities are not an MPs privilege. I personally said yesterday in the House 
that when an MP renders real justice to  a petition of an electorate, which 
includes taking the papers, scanning it, typing it,

Points arising out of answers given in Rajya Sabha on 10* August, 2006 to 
Starred Questions No.242 and 249 Regarding 'Discrimination Against Indians 
in British Jails' and 'Negotiations for release of Indians in British Jails.' 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan):  Sir, finally, I am able to 
raise this discussion on discrimination agai nst Indians in different jails all over 
the world. Sir, as per the information provided by the Government, currently, 
Indian prisoners are interned in 42 jails all over the world. Sir, in Europe and 
America, Indian prisoners are detained fo r the charges relating to immigration 
laws or serious crimes like murder or narco trade. In Germany, the local 
authorities do not provide information about murder and crime. 
Now, in different countries, the Ambassadors or the Embassies or 
the High Commission offices, they do not bother even about ordinary citizens 
who are visitors from India to those co untries. They do not bother about the 
NRIs. If they do not bother about them , how will they bother about these 
prisoners? This is the lowest priority. I would request the hon. Minister to 
please look into this aspect. They are also human beings. I am not saying that 
they will change the law. Different c ountries have different laws. Let them 
follow their laws. Those who are criminals, they should be punished. I have 
nothing against them. My only submission is that, at least, we should have 
statistics. We have computers now. On e cannot say that he does not know 
this information or that information. Maybe he does not have the information 
today, but the information should be colle cted and this should be kept all the 
time.' How many prisoners are there in different jails; what kind of crimes have 
they committed; for how long are they under-trials; do they need any kind of 
help, so that they may not remain under-trial for life? These are the things. 
How many women are there? Children may have been also in jails for different 
crimes, whether small or big.  We should

[24 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
have these statistics. They are our br others; they are our sisters. Maybe 
under different circumstances, they committed some crimes. So, we shou'd 
have these statistics.  This is what I wanted to know. 
In fact, in the U.S.A., 158 Indians are languishing in the New York 
Jail. Most of them are booked for violat ion of Immigration Laws, remaining are 
booked for crimes. How many of these are ynder-trials and for how long?  All 
these information may please be made available. 
Sir, I have come to know that in US, Indians arrested in the aftermath 
of 9/11 terrorist attacks are languish ing in Wackenhut Detention Center 
without being charged and many without access even to lawyers. I think there 
is some responsibility of our Government. They are on hunger strike. An 
Indian immigrant, Mr. Makhan Singh, is  one of the prisoners there. He has 
said in an interview that no one is eating. He has also said that he has a wife 
and two children who are American citizens. He has been in detention centre 
for six months. The Wackenhut prison , the report says, is a converted 
warehouse building with no windows in the middle of a warehouse district in

years even though no terrorism-related or other criminal charges have been 
brought against any one of them. Thes e people should be taken care of. 
There is some kind of responsibility of our Government also. 
Similarly, Sir, in Gulf region, in UAE, there are 1073 prisoners, in 
Muscat, there are 72, in Saudi Arabia, there are 1444. They are unskilled 
labourers who had gone there. They are semi-skilled. They don't have proper 
education also. They don't know for what kind of offences they have been 
jailed. So, it should be the responsib ility of our nation to look into these 
aspects. 
Sir, coming to Pakistan, there ar e 371 fishermen, 205 civilians and 
64 POWs languishing in Pakistan. Eight civilians have been languishing for 25 
years, ten for the last 20 years, 25 for the last 15 years and 27 for more than

Nehru was the Prime Minister. People could not accept the Japanese and British 
Report of Neiaji's alleged death in a plane crash at Taihoku on 18th August, 1945.

know what exactly happened to their most respectable leader, Netaji S ubhas 
Chandra Bose, after his mysterious disappearance in August, 1945. When the then 
Government was not agreeing to respond to the people's demand, people 
themselves took initiative to form a non-official Inquiry Committee, headed by the 
famous international jurist, Dr. Radha Vinod Pal. In view of this public move and

Statement-I 
Steps taken fo strengthen TPDS since 2004-05 
The Government has had several rounds of meetings with the State 
Government, Fair Price Shop Dealers Federation, and Members of 
Parliament for strengthening of the Public Distribution System in the country. 
After consultation at various levels, the Government has issued instructions 
to the States to undertake a campaign for review of Below Poverty Line 
(BPL)/Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) lists to eliminate ghost ration cards; 
take action under Clause 9 of the Public Distribution System (Control) Order 
for punishing the guilty to ensure leakage-free distribution of foodgrains; 
involve elected Panchayati Raj Institution (PRI) members in distribution of 
foodgrains; display of BPL/AAY beneficiary lists on al! Fair Price Shops 
(FPS); put up the district-wise and FPS- wise allocation of foodgrains on the 
websites ensure timely availability of foodgrains at FPS level; take up 
training of members at the FPS level; establish Vigilance Committees and 
computerize the PDS operations to ensure transparency in the system. 
Statement-Il 
Major Improvements in the functioning of the FCI since 2004-05. 
(i) Debt restructuring:- FCl has mobilized Rs. 8604.90 crore (through 
issue of bonds for Rs. 5000 crore at an average coupon rate of

7.14% and for Rs. 3604.90 crore at an average coupon rate of 
7.54%) against the bank interest rate of 8.15%. This has resulted in 
a saving of Rs. 174 crore in the food subsidy till July, 2006. 
(ii) Implementation fo Integrated Information System for Foodgrains 
Management (IISFM):- The IISFM project under implementation 
since 2004-05 aims at improving the FCI efficiency through 
computerization of foodgrains stocks at the depot and district level 
at a total cost of Rs. 97.66 crores. As on 1.5.2006 hardware had 
been supplied at all the 895 locations and installation completed at 
785 locations. So far 75% of FCI depots have started computerized 
data entry of their stocks. 
(iii) Implementation of Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS):— The 
VRS scheme was introduced by FCI for its permanent employees in 
June 2004. A total number of 8,777 employees took VRS under the 
scheme. This has resulted in reduction of establishment cost of the 
FCI by around Rs. 150 crore annually. 
(iv) McKinsey & Co. study report:- Pursuant to the recommendations 
made by M/s. McKinsey & Co. a Policy implementation Office 
(PIO) has been set up in May, 2005 with a specific mandate to 
implement efficiency improvement ideas. 
Statement III 
Expansion of Nutrition Programmes since 2004-05 
ICDS

Court's direction the Government approved expansion of the ICDS

additional Anganwadi Centres, taking the total number of ICDS 
projects from 5652 to 6118 and Anganwadi Centres from 7.58 to 
9.46 lakhs. 
(ii) The financial norms for Suppl ementary Nutrition Programme (SNP) 
have been doubled from Re. 1 to Rs. 2 per day per beneficiary and

supplementary nutrition with the States/UTs from 2005-06, against

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. 
RAJA): (a) to (c) Ganga Action Plan Phase I, the first attempt of Government 
to clean the river Ganga, was launched in the year 1985. The Plan was taken 
up to treat partial pollution load (almost 65% at that time) of the river due to 
resource crunch. Under this Plan, 259 projects of pollution abatement spread 
over 25 towns in the States of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal were 
completed leading to the creation of additional sewage treatment capacity of 
865 million litres per day (mld). The Plan was declared closed in March, 
2000. Since GAP. Phase I did not cover the pollution load of Ganga fully, 
GAP Phase II which includes plans for Yamuna, Gomti, Damodar and 
Mahananda besides Ganga was approved in stages from 1993 onwards. The 
present sanctioned cost of the works of pollution abatement for Ganga river 
under GAP Phase II is Rs. 492.16 crore against which an amount of Rs. 
251.17 crore has been released to the State implementing agencies. Out of a 
total of 271 sanctioned schemes, 80 schemes have been completed so far and 
the balance schemes are in different stages of implementation. 
With the completion of the pollution abatement works under the Ganga 
Action Plan (GAP) Phase-I (1985-2000) as well as the works undertaken 
under GAP Phase-ll (1995 onwards), notwithstanding the phenomenal 
increase in urban population leading to substantial increase in the pollution 
load of the river Ganga over the past years, water quality of river Ganga has 
shown improvement at major locations over its pre-GAP quality. A tabular 
statement in this regard is attached as per Statement (See below).

*439. SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of

including labour-intensive sectors such as auto components and textiles from 
49 per cent at present to 74 per cent;

be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHAVIR PRASAD): (a) and (b) According to the existing policy, an 
entity, domestic or foreign, without any subsisting industrial interest can 
invest upto 100% in the equity of a small scale industry (SSI) engaged in the

Work out a comprehensive medium-term strategy for food and

such regions. Review in this context all ongoing Technology

Suggest measures for enhancing the quality and cost

†3053. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that only 1.3 per cent of Gross Domestic Product 
are offered as agricultural subsidy by Government in the country whereas 
this subsidy is up to 42 per cent of the GDP in Economic Corporation and 
Development Countries; 
(b) if not, the facts in this regard; and

agri-products while competing with the agri-products of th ese countries in 
view of the above situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) As per the 
estimates of Central Statistical Organization (CSO), the agricultural subsidy 
in India as percentage of GDP at current prices accounts for about 1.06 per 
cent in the year 2004-05. As per the detabase of the Organization for 
Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries, their 
agricultural subsidy is 33.98 per cent in 2004. 
(c) The paucity of resources in a developing country like India does not 
allow to match the agricultural subsidy given by the OECD countries. In the 
ongoing negotiations on Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) in the WTO, India 
has demanded that subsidies be eliminated to create level playing field in 
trade for developing countries. To encourage exports and increase access to 
international markets, the Government implements schemes such as 
Transport Assistance Scheme and Vishesh Krishi Upaj Yojna. 
As per FAO Statistical Year book (2004), share of India's agicultural 
exports in the world rose to 1.25 percent in 2002 from 1.19 percent 
witnessed during 1999-2001 . Daring the same period, share of India's 
agricultural imports in the world rose to 0.87 percent in 2002 from 0.82

foodgrains are being flouted with impunity;

immediate remedial measures are taken. The officials found indulging in such 
activities are immediately taken to task and suitable disciplinary action 
initiated against them.

foodgrains strict norms of inspection are being implemented and as a result, 
quality complaints against the stocks procured during the current Kharif

"New Delhi as the World's Capital for e-waste recycling" 
3084. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: 
SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: 
Wiil the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to a new study, New Delhi is 
emerging as the World's Capital for e-waste recycling - a hazardous activity 
taking place without any regulations; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the annual volume of e-waste, the junk 
produced by discarded electronic equipment in Delhi is around 10,000 metric 
tones; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to introduce more 
facilities for proper recycling? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHR I NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) 
to (c) No systematic study has been carried out so far on e-waste recycling 
and annual generation of e-waste junk produced by discarded electronic 
equipment. There have, however, been some uncomfirmed reports on the 
quantum of e-waste generation in the recent past. 
The provisions under Hazardous Waste (Management and Handling) 
Rules 1989 as amended in 2000 and 2003 includeds E-waste. These rules 
regulate the generation, collection, storage, treatment, disposal, 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2006] 
export and import of ad hazardous wastes. The processes generating 
hazardous wastes are listed in schedule 1 of these rules. The residues and 
wastes generated from the operations in electronic industry are considered as 
hazardous wastes and are listed at SI. No. 31 of schedule 1 of these rules. 
Further, as per the provisions of these rules Electrical; and Electronics 
Assemblies are covered under Category B-1110 in Schedule 3 of these rules 
which are applicable for import and export of hazardous wastes. The import 
of wastes under this category are only permitted for direct reuse and not for 
recycling or final disposal. Further, the Central Pollution Control Board 
(CPCB) has undertaken a study for the preparation of a "Guideline Document 
for Environmentally Sound Recycling of E-Waste" for the State Pollution 
Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees of the Union Territories as 
well as the industries, through an expert agency having experience in this 
field. 
Crack in Gangotri Glacier 
†3085. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
SHRI KAMAL 
AKHTAR: 
WR the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a big crack has been sighted in Gangotri 
Glacier which is the place of origin of River Ganges; 
(b) If so, whether it has been proved that Himalayan glaciers have 
started melting due to global warming; 
(c) If so, whether it would pose a threat of water shortage in rivers such 
as Ganges, Indus and Brahmaputra after some years; and 
(d) If, so what steps are being taken by Govemment to face this situation? 
THE MINIISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) The Crack observed 
in Gangotri Glacier near the originating place of the Ganga River is not a 
new observation. It had been observed in Aerial Photographs of October 
1960 and 1962. The origin of these cracks can be attributed to the neo 
tectonics activity. Such cracks are not conclusive evidence of melting of  
glaciers due to global warming. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
130 

[25 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) As for the phenomenon of global warming resulting in melting of 
glaciers, the scientific studies have revealed that glaciers of Himalayan 
region are passing through a phase of recession (shrinking) as is the case 
with the glaciers elsewhere in the world at variable rates due to a variety of 
reasons like macro and micro climate, reduction in snow fall, and size of 
glaciers. Cracks in a glacier are developed due to stress build up within a 
glacier. 
(c) The scientific studies do not suggest threat of water shortage in the 
rivers in the foreseeable future. 
(d) Since the recession of glaciers is a natural process and is not 
attributable to any one meteorological parameter, the components of 
mitigation strategy comprise monitoring of the glaciers, expansion and 
diversification of the meteorological observation network, reduction in 
deforestation, and preservation of ecology in high altitudes. The G.B. Pant 
Institute of Himalayan Environment and Development (GBPIHED) has been 
conducting studies on Gangotri glacier systems for the last seven years, 
which do not indicate significant melt water discharge. The State 
Government of Uttaranchal has set up an Expert Committee for glacier 
conservation measures.

Improvement in quality of water in India 
3 0 9 5 .    D R .    M . A . M .    R A M A S W A M Y :    W i l l   t h e   M i n i s t e r   o f  
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the quality of water in India is among the 
worst in the world; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the main pollutants which are carried by Indian rivers; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to improve the quality of water in 
Indian rivers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHR I NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) 
and (b) The water quality of rivers in India is determined through a set of 
parameters based on the designated-best-use of river stretches. Under the 
National Water Quality Monitoring Network, the Central Pollution Control 
Board has identified 71 polluted stretches on different rivers in the country 
based on the data of Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), an indicator of 
organic pollution. No comparative study has, however, been made on the 
quality of water in India with that in the world 
(c) Rivers in India are polluted mainly due to the discharge of treated & 
untreated municipal and industrial wastewaters, resulting mainly in increased 
organic mater measured in terms of BOD and microbial pollution indicated 
by the coliform counts. Agricultural run off and other non-point sources of 
pollution like open defecation, run off from solid wastes dumps sites etc., 
also contribute to water quality deterioration through addition of nitrogen, 
phosphorus- and other trace organic compounds. 
(d) The pollution abatement for Indian rivers was initiated with the 
implementation of the Ganga Action Plan (GAP-I) in the year 1985. Under 
this plan, 259 projects were completed in 25 towns of Utter Pradesh, Bihar 
and West Bengal. The second phase of Ganga Action Plan was taken up in 
stages from 1993 to 1998 and was later re-named as National River 
Conservation Plan (NRCP). Presently, NRCP covers pollution 
138 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
abatement works in 160 towns spread over 20 states and 34 rivers in the 
country. The plan involves implementation of pollution abatement works 
namely, interception & diversion of sewage, setting up of sewage treatment 
plants, low cost sanitation, crematoria and river front development. So far, a 
total of 2598 million liters per day of sewage treatment facility has been 
created under these plans to improve the water quality. The Industrial 
pollution under the Plan is tackled by the Central Pollution Control Board 
and its state counterparts through the implementation of legal provisions 
under the Water (Prevention & Pollution Control) Act, 1974 and 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

• Minor environmental engineering  
(iii) Supporting Interventions: 
• Behaviour Change Communication 
• Public-Private Partnership & Inter-sectoral convergence 
• Human Resource Development through capacity building 
• Operational research including studies on drug resistance and 
insecticide susceptibility

Guidelines for human clinical trials 
3108. SHR! P.R. RAJAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) have 
conducted any survey regarding the guidelines followed by the Indian 
Institutional Committees during human clinical trials; 
(b) if so, the details including number and the details of the Institutional 
Committees which are not following the guidelines; 
(c) if so, the action taken, if any, against the Institutional Committees 
for violation of the guidelines; and 
(d) the details of number of clinical trials convened in the country for 
last three years, year-wise, category-wise and State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to(c) 
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has issued Ethical Guidelines 
for clinical research on human subjects including clinical trials of drugs, 
diagnostics and vaccines in 1980 which was revised in 2000. According to 
these guidelines all institutions doing clinical research should have an 
institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) forgiving approval for these studies. 
Under the Drug and Cosmetic Act also all institutions should have Ethics 
Committee approval before initiating the trial in addition to other provisions 
for clinical trials. The Indian Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines 2002 
149 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2006] 
and the Schedule Y for clinical trials also give detailed requirements. ICMR 
conducted a survey of Institutional Ethics Committee during 2003-04. Out of 
the 233 institutions who responded, 178 had lECs. ICMR and GCP 
guidelines prescribed the structure and procedures to be followed by the 
lECs. The survey indicated that by and large the existing Committees are 
constituted as per the guidelines. Steps have already been initiated to 
legislate the ICMR Ethical Guidelines into an Act so that it becomes 
mandatory that all institutions doing clinical research should have IEC as per 
proposed norms. 
(d) There are 200 clinical trials approved by regulatory authority 
received in the last three years. Category-wise and State-wise information 
about these clinical trials is not maintained. 
Hepatitis Vaccine 
†3109. SHRI KRISHAN LAL BALMIKI: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the Hepatitis disease 
is taking a serious turn by taking more and more people in its grip. 
(b) whether Government hospitals are well equipped with the Hepatitis 
vaccine; and 
(c) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) 
There are five common types of Hepatitis, viz., A, B, C, D and E. Hepatitis—
A is benign as compared to others. Out of the remaining four, there is 
vaccine only for prevention of Hepatitis B. India has the second largest pool 
of Hepatitis B virus (HBV) carriers in the world and contributes to nearly 
15% of the entire pool of HBV carriers in the world. 
Hepatitis B is preventable by ensuring precautionary measures, 
including vaccination. The Government has launched a pilot project for 
immunization against Hepatitis B free of cost for children below one year 
only. Hepatitis B vaccination has commenced and is continuing in 15 cities 
since 2002-03 and in 32 districts and in Andaman & Nicobar islands since 
2003-04. Besides, vaccine for Hepatitis B is available in the country at 
affordable prices.

SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to

(a) whether Government have taken cognizance of continuing rise in 
cases of diabetes and cardio-vascular diseases; 
(b) whether Government have launched any programme to contain these 
diseases and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(c) if so, the details of these programmes and what are the tangible 
targets set for these programmes;

(e) what are the modalities to periodically monitor the performance

and how does Government propose to generate these resources? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (f) 
Yes, Sir. The diabetes and cardiovascular diseases are increasing in India. 
The exact number of people having heart diseases is not known. According 
to the revised estimates of WHO, India has approximately 32 million people 
with diabetes and projected to touch 57.2 million in 2025. There is a increase 
in prevalence of Ischaemic Heart Disease (IHD) in urban areas in India. The 
prevalence of IHD has increased considerably during last decade, especially 
in urban areas. Although there is increase in prevalence of ischaemic heart 
disease in rural areas also, but it is not all that steep. 
The Government proposes to initiate and implement a "National 
Programme for the Prevention and Control of Diabetes, Cardio-vascular 
diseases (CVD) and Stroke" to reduce the adverse health impact of diabetes, 
heart diseases and Stroke. Under this proposed National Programme IEC will 
be one of the major components to sensitise the public about the dangerous 
effect of these diseases and the need for prevention.

FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the outbreak of various diseases 
in various parts of the country are mainly due to very poor disease

inadequate functioning of the district surveillance units; 
166 

[25 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the effective steps proposed to be taken

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) 
Disease surveillance is primarily the responsibility of the State Government. 
The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State to combat the 
outbreak of diseases. A National Surveillance Programme for Communicable 
Diseases (NSPCD) was implemented in 101 districts in the year 1997 for 
augmenting the surveillance activities. 
Further, Integrated Disease Surv eillance Project (IDSP) has been 
launched in November 2004 as a Centrally sponsored scheme with the 
objective to integrate disease surveillane activities in the country. Disease 
Surveillance would provide essential data to detect early warning signals of 
impending outbreaks and epidemics and to facilitate timely and effective 
response to crub spread of diseases. The project would be implemented by 
State Surveillance units and District Surveillance units. 
IDSP is being introduced is phased manner as detailed below: 
Phase I (2004-05) 9 States, namely, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, 
Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh, Kerala, Mizoram and all the 101 districts covered under the pilot 
project 'National Surveillance Programme for Communicable diseases'. 
Phase II (2005-06) 14 States/UTs, namely, Gujarat, Haryana, Rajasthan, 
Orissa, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Delhi, Goa, Chandigarh, Pondicherry, 
Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland and Tripura. 
Phase III (2006-07) Remaining States/UTs, under IDSP, the district level 
is the focus for integrating surveillance functions and Districts. Surveillance 
Units have been formed in all the districts of Phase I States and other districts 
of Phase II & III States are being covered in phased 
manner.

connectivity in the officer of Chief District Health Officer.

early to evaluate the outcomes of implementation of schemes under NRHM.

Understanding (MoU) with the States, with clear commitment of the States in 
achieving definite milestones. The status of implementation of the Mission is 
reviewed on a regular basis by this Ministry through interactions with the 
states. Senior Officers from the GOL are also deputed to visit the states to 
review the progress. Achievements are matched against the agreed 
performance indicators and timelines. The fund flow and fund utilization are 
regularly reviewed. Periodic surveys are carried out to find out the outcomes

help of credible NGOs/institutions.

Package for revival off sick SSIs in Rajasthan 
3182. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govemment have proposed to give any financial package 
and incentives for revival of sick small scale industries in Rajasthan; 
(b) if so, the amount allocated for this purpose by Govemment during 
2005-06 and current year; 
(c) the funds released by Govemment, so far; 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2006] 
(d) the results achieved thereof; and 
(e) the total number of small scale industries and how many of them 
were sick as on 31st March, 2005, and as a result of financial package and 
incentives, how many have been revived upto date? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHAVIR PRASAD): (a) to (d) The Central Government (in the Ministry 
of Small Scale Industries) does not provide any direct financial assistance for 
rehabilitation of sick SSIs. However, financial assistance, by way of debt 
restructuring, including fresh loans, for the rehabilitation of sick SSI units is 
provided by the primary lending institutions (PLI), including commercial 
banks, which provide credit to the SSI. For this purpose, the Reserve Bank of 
India (RBI) has issued detailed guidelines to banks in January, 
2002 on early detection of sickness in SSI at an early stage and taking 
remedial measures and for rehabilitation of sick SSI units identified as 
potentially viable. 
RBI has issued fresh guidelines on 8th September,2005, based on the 
"Policy package for Stepping up Credit to Small and Medium Enterprises 
(SMEs)" announced by the Central Government on 10th August2005. These 
guidelines relate, inter alia, to viability criteria, prudential norms for 
restructured accounts, provision of additional finance and time frame for 
working out the restructuring package and its implementation. 
Banks have been advised by the RBI to review the progress of 
rehabilitation and restructuring of SME accounts on a quarterly basis. The 
State Level Inter-Institutional Committee (SLIIC), set up in each State under 
the convenorship of the RBI representative, also monitors, inter alia, the 
implementation of these guidelines. 
Further, a special package of incentives for identification/revival of sick 
industrial units under the Rajasthan Investment Promotion Scheme, 
2003 has been announced by the State Government in 2004-05. 
(e) The total number of SSI units (both registered and unregistered) in 
Rajasthan as at the end of March 2005 was estimated at 4,97,712. As per the 
data compiled by the RBI from scheduled commercial banks, the number of 
sick SSI units in Rajasthan as at the end of March 2005 was 2,241. Out of 14 
sick SSI units identified as potentially viable, 1 unit was put under nursing at 
the end of March 2005. Further, under the special package of the State 
Government, 12 sick industrial units have been covered so far. 
Steps for development of small scale sector 
3183. SHRI N. R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
218 

[25 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) the details of the new schemes launched by the Government to 
promote and develop small scale industries along with the assistance/ 
subsidy extended to the entrepreneure; 
(b) the extent to which the small scale industries have been able to adjust 
in the changing scenario of economic liberation and globalisation by these 
new schemes; and 
(c) the other steps taken by Government for the development of small 
scale sector? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHAVIR PRASAD): (a) The development and promotion of small scale 
industries is primarily the responsibility of the respective State/Union 
Territory (UT) Government/administrations. The Central Government, 
however, support and supplements the efforts of the State Government/UT 
Administrations through various schemes/programmes relating to credit, 
performance and credit rating, infrastructural development, technology 
upgradation, marketing, entrepreneurial development, etc. These are 
implemented across the country. The details of the relatively new schemes 
along with the assistance/subsidy extended to the entrepreneurs are listed in 
the Statement (See Below). 
(b) The Central Government constantly assesses and monitors the 
impact of the liberalization/globalisation and changing economic scenario on 
the growth and the development of the economy, including that of small 
scale industries (SSIs) in the country. Measures taken by the Government 
from time to time for the promotion and development of small scale 
industries and to enhance their competitiveness have helped them to compete 
in the global as well as domestic markets, as is evident from their growth in 
terms of number of units and contribution to national production, 
employment generation and exports. 
(c) Government has put in place several measures to help small 
enterprises. These included schemes of assistance for technology 
upgradation, infrastructure development, cluster development, adoption of 
modern management practices, marketing, etc. Further, steps have been 
taken to enhance credit flow to the SSI units, sensitise them to matters 
relating to global trade liberalization and facilitate information dissemination 
through the use of information technology. To facilitate cost reduction 
design process improvement and product diversification to make the Indian 
SSl product competitive, the Central Government has modernized its 
Process-cum-Product Development Centres (PPDCs) and Tool Rooms. In 
addition, the field offices of Small Industries Development Organisation 
(SIDO), i.e., Small Industries Services Insititution (SIS,) have set up 
Technology Resource Centres (TRCs) to advise and enable the SSIs to 
upgrade themselves so as to compete in the global market.

Bringing steel research and training institutes under an organisation 
3185. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government, in a bid to meet the growing 
technical and human resource requirements of the steel industry, are planning 
to bring all existing steel research and training institutes under an umbrella 
organisation and also plan to almost double its funding for research and 
development activities in the steel sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when the proposal is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. 
AKHILESH DAS): (a) to (c) No, Sir. wh ile it has been envisaged in the 
National Steel Policy (NSP) that the existing training and research institutes 
under the Ministry of Steel would be brought under an umbrella organization 
with representation from each segment of the industry, but similarly placed 
institutes in the private sector would continue to maintain their independent 
existence.

3186. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Wi ll the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the annual production of iron ore by pub[ic 
sector companies is far below than that of the private sector companies; 
(b) if so, the details thereof during the last five years and the reasons 
therefor; 
(c) the details of plant utilisation capacity of public sector companies 
during the last five years, plant-wise; and 
(d) the efforts being made to produce more and more iron ore in the 
country so as to compete with private players? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. 
AKHILESH DAS) : (a) and (b) Yes Sir. However,   it is a recent 
233

phenomenon. The production of iron ore by the public sector and private 
sector during the last five years is given as under: 
(Quantity in million tonnes)  
Year Public Sector Private Sector

2002-03 49.69 49.37

(Source : IBM, Nagpur) 
 
The significant higher production by private sector during 2003-04 and 
2004-05 is on account of unexpected and huge demand from China. The 
export of iron ore from India is mainly in the form of fines.lt is mainly the 
private sector which is involved in the export of iron ore. If the Chinese 
demand declines, the Indian miners will find their markets for fines 
dwindling. The SME sector mines will once again reduce their operation or 
become inactive. 
(c) The details of capacity utilization of the mines of Steel Authority of 
India Limited (SAIL), National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd.

South Block (Kiriburu) and Central Block (Meghathaburu). It will also 
expand its Bolani iron ore mine. NMDC has also made plans to increase the 
production of iron ore from the pres ent level of around 23 million tonne 
during 2005-06 to 32 million tonne by the year 2009-10. KIOCL was in 
possession of only one iron ore mine at Kudremukh in the State of

UNDP help to steel sector 
3187. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of STEEL be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that steel has been identified as major consumer of 
CTC and that SAIL has been offered UNDP help, the officials of which have 
also visited SAIL plants to implement to phase out CTC to freeze and reduce 
the ozone depleting substances; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the action plan for different plants during 2006-07 and 2007-08; and 
(d) the steps taken by other steel plants in private sector in this regard? 
236 

[25 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. 
AKHILESH DAS): (a) and (b), Yes, Sir. Six Plants of Steel Authority of 
India Limited (SAIL) in the Steel Sector were identified as consumers of 
Carbon tetrachloride (CTC) by an international consultant alongwith local 
UNDP representatives who had visited these plants and financial assistance 
was recommended for implementation of measures under the Montreal 
Protocol through the Government of Japan to phase out consumption of CTC 
for non-feedstock application in a time bound manner. Major equipment 
have been received at New Delhi for the use of SAIL steel plants. 
(c) The erection & commissioning of equipment and training for 
operating the equipment have been planned during 2006-07 & 2007-08. 
(d) As per available information, none of the main/major steel plants in 
the private sector are using CTC. No information in this regard however is 
available in respect of large number of mini steel plants or steel processing 
units.

STATEMENTS BY MINISTERS 
Outcome of Enquiry into Alleged Conversation by Shri Manik Rao 
H. Gavit, Minister of State in the Ministry of Home Affairs, with a 
Jail inmate in Bulandshahar Jail 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The Home Minister, Shri Shivraj V. Patil, to make a 
statement regarding the findings of the Enquiry Committee into the veracity of 
Zee news telecast dated 13th August, 2006 on Shri Manikrao Gavit, Minister 
of State in the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): Sir, on 
13.8.2006 Zee TV Channel, by using an audio tape, alleged that Mr. Gavit, 
the Minister of State, Home Affairs, had conversation with a criminal in 
Bulandshahar jail. The allegation was repeated for hours in the day. 
Mr. Gavit, made a statement in the Lok Sabha and also in the Rajya 
Sabha, asserting in essence that, he had not at any time, spoken to any 
criminal in Bulandshahar jail, and that, the voice on the tape played by the 
Zee T.V. Channel, was not that of his, and that, what was shown or hear, on 
the said T.V. channel, was baseless, false, and fabricated, and that he did not 
know the person to whom it was alleged that he had spoken. 
He stated that he was willing to subject himself in any manner to any 
inquiry by anybody or by a committee of the Parliament to ascertain the truth 
in the matter, and that he would refrain from discharging his executive or 
legislative functions, until the report of the inquiry was given to the House, and 
he would not join his duties unless he was acquitted. 
254 

[25 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
He also had stated that, he was willing to accept any punishment, if any 
iota of evidence was found to fix the guilt on him, and was willing to renounce 
his political life, if he was found guilty. He had requested that the inquiry 
should be conducted in an expeditious manner avoiding unnecessary delays. 
It appears that in a committee meeting of representatives of Parliamentary 
Parties, it was decided that the matter should be inquired into by the 
Government, and the report could be given by it to the House. A letter 
indicating this in essence was sent to the hon. Prime Minister by the hon. 
Speaker. The letter suggested that the report should be given expeditiously 
possibly by 25th of August, 2006. 
In pursuance of the said letter, the CBI was asked to inquire in the matter 
and give the report before the Parliament was adjourned sine die on 25th 
August, 2006. 
The CBI collected the tapes from the Zee TV. and recorded the 
statements of the relevant persons and collected the voice of Mr. Gavit on the 
tape in the presence of independent witnesses and experts from Central 
Forensic Science Laboratory, Delhi and recorded his statement. 
The relevant tapes were sent to the Central Forensic Science Laboratory 
to compare the voices on the tapes to find out if they tallied and to give a 
report, if they were of one and the same person or different persons. The 
voices on the tapes were examined on audio spectrography by the experts 
who have opined that they do not tally and are not of the same person. The 
expert report is authenticated and laid on the Table of the House. 
The matter at this state is brought to the notice of the House.

Demand for Exemplary Penalty for Hoax Callers 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA (Rajasthan): I commend the attention of 
this House to the new ominous trend of hoax calls, Emails in the wake of 
recent terror attacks. Despite earnest appeals by the authorities against 
rumour mongering, a few persons have deliberately chosen to trivialise what 
is truly an alarming situation for the internal security. As the security forces try 
to pursue the leads of such hoax calls and mails, such misinformation actually 
derail the investigations as police lose vital time and dues. Such acts not only 
mislead the investigations but also put extra pressure over the security 
agencies. As such, these persons, irrespective of their motive and age should 
be considered as an active accomplice in the acts of terrorism and should be 
given exemplary penalty. The Government must ascertain their antecedents 
and linkages. Also, the media should not give credence to those persons who 
seek to derive media publicity through such acts. The media too should evolve 
its own norms to distinguish between sensitising the public against terrorism 
and sensationalising the terrorism. Excessive media-coverage of terrorism 
only creates a sieged psyche in the country and serves the purpose of 
terrorists. I call upon the Government to issue guidelines for the telecom 
companies, PCOs and Internet kiosks, in consultation with police and 
intelligence authorities and telecommunications experts. To ensure 
compliance of such guidelines, the Government should also take steps to train 
district-level police to trace cyber crimes.

Concern over excess Fluoride in drinking water in Karbi-Anglong District 
of Assam 
SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA (Assam): The Karbi-Anglong district of 
Assam is hit by the excess intake of fluoride contained water. The maximum 
permissible limit of fluoride in one litre of water is only 1.5 mg. But in some 
parts of the district, the fluoride content found is 15.6 mg which may cause 
non-curable diseases to human life. Fluoride was first detected in 1999 in 
Karbi-Anglong, and the All India Hygiene and Public Health Laboratory at 
Kolkata confirmed the very high level of fluoride in drinking water. The 
minimum level of fluoride content is found to be 1.6 mg. and maximum level is 
16 mg. Within the district, people of Karbi-Anglong are deprived of pure 
drinking water. Various schemes adopted by the State PHE are not 
successful, and the money already spent for the supply of fluoride free 
drinking water to the people has not been utilised properly. It is noticed that 
the people of the district are suffering from various diseases, like deficiency of 
vitamins and Gastroenteritis. The State Health Department has done analysis 
and warned that if immediate measures are not taken to provide pure drinking 
water to the people, it may cause serious problem to the people in the near 
future. Therefore, Government's attention is drawn towards that problem and, I 
uvge, upon the Government to take immediate action in this regard with a view 
to make the district a fluoride-free district and to provide pure drinking water.

Request for Forest Department's clearance for laying a road between 
Thevaram and Sakkulathumettu in Tamil Nadu 
SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I wish to bring to the notice 
of the Government about the urgent need for laying a five kilometre long road 
in the forest land between Thevaram and Sakkulathumettu in Theni district of 
Tamil Nadu. It is a link road which connects Tamil Nadu with Kerala. It is a 
long-pending demand of the people of both the States, Tamil Nadu and 
Kerala. Now the people of both the States are using a circuitous route to 
reach their destinations. The five kilometre long road could be formed through 
forest land. But ever time, the Forest Department is denying permission for 
the road formation citing many reasons. Due to this attitude of the Forest 
Department, the formation of a new road is not taking place. If this road is 
formed, it will reduce journey time considerably. It will be very useful not only 
for the public but also for the traders of both the States. I appeal to the 
Central Government, through this House, to intervene in this matter and urge 
upon the Forest Department to relax the rules for the formation of five 
kilometres road between Thevaram and Sakkulathumettu at an early date. 
This will facilitate passenger traffic and goods' movements between Tamil 
Nadu and Kerala by reducing time and fare, besides promoting trade and 
business.

Need to Speed Up Clearance of Cheques by Banks 
SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, generally, the banks 
clear the cheques deposited by customers in four to six days. 
However, a recent study, conducted by the Indian Statistical Institute and 
the Reserve Bank of lndia, has found that a large volume of the customer 1 
cheques get inordinately delayed in clearance; and due to this delayed 
clearance, the banks—public sector, private and foreign-enriched themselves 
by about Rs. 3,726 crores during the year 2005-06. The enrichment had been 
on some 13,000 lakh cheques, worth Rs. 113,37,000 crores. The banks 
enjoyed "free float of customer funds" on 50 per cent of the cheques 
transacted. 
Sir, the outstation cheques, in particular, have become a virtual nightmare 
for the customers. While chequew between two State capitals take 10-14 days 
for clearance, those from the hinterland may not be realised by the customers 
for months. 
Most of the banks have not yet put in place their cheque collection and 
clearance policy, and the chaos has led to the violation of consumers' right to 
access their funds in time; and the non-payment of interest or any other 
compensation following the delays, had led to the banks' undue enrichment on 
free float of customers' funds. 
Sir, in order to protect the consumers' rights, and also to speed up the 
tempo of business transactions, it is necessary to streamline the procedures 
and lay down suitable norms for easy and quick clearance of local and 
outstation cheques. With Internet banking-technology tools now available, 
banks can credit even the outstation cheques instantaneouly.

Plight of Poultry Farmers In the Country 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I rise to draw 
the attention of this House towards heavy losses being suffered by farmers 
due to bird flue scare. There is an urgent need to release five lakh tons of 
maize for the farmers of the country at the rate of Rs. 3500/ - per ton, as 
agreed upon by the Government immediately as the farmers are in great 
distress. The Ministry of Agriculture has already announced the relief, which is 
yet to reach the farmers. It may be mentioned that the poultry sector accounts 
for about two per cent of the GDP of India and about ten per cent of the total 
GNP attributable to livestock. With annual output of 37 billion eggs and 1,000 
million broilers, which yield 5.75 lakh tonnes of poultry meat, India is the fourth 
highest producer of eggs and the eighth highest producer of broilers in the 
world. The broiler production has sky-rocketed at an annual growth rate of 
about ten per cent and stands at about 1.9 million metric tonnes of chicken 
meat (FAO 2005). Besides, this sector provides large self-employment 
opportunities to a number of people in urban and rural areas. Since the poultry 
industry has been making considerable contribution to the national economy, 
it needs immediate attention and support at this hour of crisis. I, therefore, call 
upon the Government to take affirmative and corrective steps, without further 
loss of time, to provide all assistance to farmers and save poultry industry 
from total collapse.

Request to Direct GAIL to Refund Excess Gas Transportation Charges 
Levied on Gas-based Projects in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, GAIL has been 
supplying gas to gas-based power projects of Thatipaka-Kakinada, Thatipaka-
Kovuru and Thatipaka-Kondapally in Andhra Pradesh, and, as a part of the 
agreement, the State has to pay transportation charges. But, for the reasons 
best known to GAIL, it has imposed Rs. 606.78 crores more transportation 
charges on the above gas-based projects between 1996-97 and 2004-05. 
But, in spite of the Government of Andhra Pradesh's requests, GAIL has 
refused to reduce the excess transportation charges levied by it. Then, the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh went before the Tariff Commission indicating 
how GAIL overcharged for gas supplied to plants in Andhra Pradesh. The 
Tariff Commission has decided that GAIL has overcharged the transportation 
cost from Andhra Pradesh recently. The Tariff Commission has calculated the 
costs as per the Cost of Service. According to this, GAIL has overcharged Rs. 
444.08 crores on the gas supplied through Thatipaka-Kakinada gas pipeline, 
Rs. 47.64 crores through Thatipaka-Kovuru gas pipeline and Rs. 116.06 
crores through Thatipaka-Kondapall y gas pipeline, apart from other 
miscellaneous charges. GAIL has charged 175 per cent more to two gas-
based projects, 400 per cent more to one project and 150 per cent more to 
the fourth project. Now, the Tariff Commission has already submitted its 
Report to the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. The Government of 
India also opined that GAIL does not have any fixed method of calculating the 
transportation cost. Hence, I request the Government of India to immediately 
direct GAIL to refund the excess amount collected by it or adjust in the future 
transportation charges.

VALEDICTORY REMARKS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, we come to the end of the 208th 
Session which had commenced on Monday, the 24th of July. We have had 22 
sittings spread over a period of 33 days. In this Section, the monsoon 
showers helped us to keep the 'heaf under control and generally provided us 
a pleasant environment conducive to transaction of serious business by the 
House - though, at times, it was felt that more of these showers were needed! 
In this Session, seven new Members joined us arid one got re-elected. I 
do hope that they will make meaningful contributions in enriching the 
proceedings of the House. 
This Session has been lively as well as busy; Members often sitting till 
the late hours of the evening and even foregoing the lunch break to transact 
important business. 
Hon. Members, you are aware that in the previous Session, this august 
House had passed the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Amendment 
Bill, 2006. This Bill was returned by the hon. President of India with his 
message to Parliament. The matter was given serious consideration by the 
House and a very enligthened debate took place 
288 

 [25 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
before the Bill was passed again by this august House. Subsequently, the 
House also resolved to constitute a Joint Parliamentary Committee to 
examine and consider important issues relating to the provisions of this Bill. 
The House transacted important Legislative Business, including 
consideration and passing of 16 Bills. I would, particularly, like to mention the 
Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Bill, 2005, the Juvenile Justice 
(Care and Protection of Children) Amendment Bill, 2006, the Food Safety and 
Standard Bill, 2006, the Wild Life (Protection) Admendment Bill, 2005, and the 
Essential Commodities (Amendment) Bill, 2005. The passing of these Bills 
will, no doubt, provide the requisite fillip to improve and strengthen the policy 
framework leading to improved public governance. 
Hon. Members, I am happy to note that in this Session also, you showed 
great sense of responsibility towards matters of urgent concern as well as 
problems of the people. Several wide-ranging issues were discussed and 
debated during Short Duration Discussions, Half-an-Hour Discussions or 
Calling Attentions. In addition, about 100 Special Mentions on diverse 
subjects of public importance were made by the hon. Members. 
Hon. Members, the House witnessed the expression of great concern by 
all sections on the rise in prices and the unfortunate suicide by farmers. I 
myself have been greatly concerned with the plight of more than one-fourth of 
our population still living Below the Poverty Line who are denied their 
fundamental right to live with dignity. The tragic happenings in our poor rural 
homes are indeed a matter of great concern shared by all of us. I do hope the 
serious discussion we had in this House on this subject will definitely lead to 
purposeful initiatives of action with positive results. 
This House has also been deeply concerned about the security situation 
in the country. Hon. Members were extremely saddened with the deaths 
caused due to the serial bomb blasts in Mumbai and terrorist attacks in 
Jammu and Kashmir. Serious concern was also expressed on the increasing 
Naxal violence, particularly the Naxalite attacks on relief camps at Dantewada 
in Chhattisgarh. I do hope that the serious debate and discussion on the issue 
of security and terrorism would furthe r strengthen our wi ll for determined 
action to overpower the enemies of peace and progress.

debated in the House. I would particularly mention the very satisfying debate 
of exceptional quality and high standard of excellence on the subject of

and comprehensive discussion on all aspects of the issue has been extremely 
enligtening not only to all sections of the House but also to he general public 
which, I am confident, is now better informed about the intricate aspects of 
this important matter, l believe that serious and purposeful discussion in the 
House not only brings out transparency of actions but goes to build up public

Hon. Members, I compliment you for doing a lot of business during the 
Session. However, you wiil agree with me that much more could have been

THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Hon. Chairman, Sir, 
as this Session comes to an end, we can look back with some satisfaction at 
the amount of work that has been accomplished despite the turbulence which 
characterised this Session. Sir, You have yourself mentioned that we must 
explore ways and means of improving the effectiveness of processes of 
governance and that must also include improving the functioning of 
parliamentary institution. 
Now that the television cameras focus on the activities of Parliament 
constantly, it becomes all the more necessary for Parliament to find effective 
ways and means to improve our functioning so that the Houses of Parliament 
truly become the role-model for the functioning of our Parliamentary 
democracy at large. 
Sir, sixteen important Bills have been passed; important issues have 
been discussed. If, despite tensions and turbulence, which characterised our 
deliberations, so much has been accomplished. Sir, the primary credit goes to 
you for the leadership that you have provided to all of us in the process of 
conducting this Legislative Business. I join Sushmaji to place

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2006] 
on record the outstanding services you have rendered to the Rajya Sabha 
during these four years that you have been guiding the work and the 
functioning of Rajya Sabha. Sir, we will not be meeting when your birthday 
comes on 23rd October. So, I take this opportunity to give you, Sir, our 
warmest greetings and best wishes. May God bless you with many, many 
years of productive service to our country. 
Sir, as I said, we have accomplished important business. The Economic, 
political and security situation received considerable amount of attention on 
the part of Members of this House. As you yourself have said, the standard of 
debate, particularly on the nuclear issue, I think, is something in which we can 
take legitimate pride. Similarly, issues of farmers, issues of prices, issues 
arising out the of Mumbai bomb blasts, terrorism and the situation in Jammu 
and Kashmir, all these are issues of vital concern, and that the House was 
able to deliberate, debate and discuss these issues, I think, strengthens one's 
confidence in the effectiveness of our Parliament as an instrument for voicing 
the felt needs and aspirations of our people. The Bills, that have been passed, 
also have profound implications. I would draw particular attention to the Bills 
that we have passed with regard to the Food Safety Act. In our country, when 
it comes to food processing or agro processing activities, we have just 
touched the surface. I think there is a vast scope of creating new jobs through 
development of agro processing activities in our country. This was a Bill which 
was pending for a long time. Industry and trade have been demanding it for a 
long time. That we were able to pass this very important Bill, which has a very 
important bearing on future growth, on an important segment of our economy, 
I think, is something which gives me very considerable satisfaction. On issues 
arising out of the Office of Profit Bill and the message of the President, the 
way the debate was conducted, I should say that it was a high quality debate. 
While passing the Bill again, we have actually had the wisdom to reflect on the 
longer term issues; that we have set up a Joint Parliamentary Committe to 
took at the issues which are reflected in the message of our President, I think, 
also speaks volumes of the role that an alert Parliament can play in 
safeguarding the vital interests of our nation. 
Sir, this is not an occasion to find fault with our functioning or of any 
section of the House, Sushmaji referred to the lack of debate on the KBK 
segment of Orissa. I can assure the House and the people of Orissa that their 
interests are entirely safe in the hands of this Government. There is

no attempt being made to reduce the development assistance that is being 
given to the KBK areas. This, I think, is a disinformation  campaign, and I 
sincerely hope that the true facts will be made known to the people. I myself 
am going, in a few days, to Orissa. And, therefore, I look forward to going to 
the KBK area because this  is one of the most backward regions of our 
country. It requires all the attention that both the Central and the State 
Government can give and we shall not be found wanting in response to 
development aspirations and needs of the people of Orissa, or, for that 
matter, the KBK region. 
Sir, in conclusion, I once again express to you our profound respect and 
regard for the guidance, for the outstanding quality of leadership that you 
have provided to this House. I take this opportunity to thank the Deputy 
Chairman, the Panel of Vice-Chairmen, the hon. Leader of the Opposition, 
the Secretary-General and the staff of the Rajya Sabha for all their dedicative 
work which has contributed so much to the success of this Session. I thank 
you, Sir.

THE PARLIAMENTARY DEBATES OFFICIAL REPORT IN THE 
TWO HUNDRED AND NINTH SESSION OF THE RAJYASABHA 
Commencing on the 22nd November, 2006/1 Agrahayana, 1928 (Saka)  

RAJYA SABHA  
Wednesday, the 22nd November, 2006/1 Agrahayana, 1928 (Saka)  
The House met at eleven of the clock, 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair. 
(The National Anthem, "Jana Gana Mana", was played.) 
____________  
OBITUARY REFERENCES  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with pro found 
sorrow to the passing away of Shri Sriman Prafulla Goswami, 
Shrimati Lalitha Rajagopalan, Shri Ahmad Hossain Mo ndal, Shri 
Kanshi Ram, former Members and Shri Lalit Suri, a s itting Member 
and Shri Santosh Kumar Sahu, a former Member of this House. 
[MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
Shri Sriman Prafulla Goswami passed away on 27th Ju ne, 2006, 
at the age of 96 years. He represented the State of  Assam in this 
House for two terms from May, 1967 to April, 1972 a nd again from 
April, 1974 to April, 1980. 
Bom at Nalbari, Assam in February, 1911, Shri Goswa mi had his 
education at Cotton College, Guwahati; Jorhat Colle ge and the 
Banaras Hindu University. 
Asocial worker, Shri Goswami participated in the fr eedom 
movement in the year 1921 at a very tender age. He left his studies in 
1930 and started 'Assam Pratishan', an institution for social service. 
He was convicted for joining the Anti-war Satyagrah a movement 
started by Gandhiji and imprisoned and interned sev eral times for 
participating in revolutionary activities in 1941. 
31  

RAJYASABHA [22 November, 2006] 
Shri Goswami was associated with various social, we lfare and 
educational organizations in various capacities and  worked for the 
rural reconstruction and spread of education, espec ially for girls. He 
was instrumental in organizing many Girls' and Boys ' High Schools 
and some dispensaries. He was also President of Gop althan 
Polytechnical Institution in Nalbari sub-division c ontinuously for about 
30 years since its foundation. He was deputed on ma ny occasions by 
the Government of Assam to visit hill areas of Assa m including 
Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram to study va rious problems 
at the time of crisis till 1964 and also conducted the famous "Naga 
Goodwill Mission" in Assam. Shri Goswami also serve d as the 
Chairman of the Oil India Limited from June, 1972 to June, 1974. 
Shri Goswami was a member of the Indian delegation to the 
Fourteenth Session of the United Nations and was al so part of the 
Indian delegation to the Top management Symposium c onvened by 
the Asian Productivity organization at Tokyo in 1973. 
The Legislative career of Shri Goswami had started when he was 
elected as a Member of the Assam Legislative Assemb ly in 1952. He 
again got elected to that Assembly in 1962. 
In the passing away of Shri Sriman Prafulla Goswami , the country 
has lost a veteran Parliamentarian and a dedicated social worker. 
Shrimati Lalitha Rajagopalan passed away on the 5th  August, 
2006, at the age of 83 years. 
Bom at Madras in March, 1924 Shrimati Rajagopalan h ad her 
education at Presidency High School, Pachiappa's Co llege and 
Women's Christian College, Madras. 
Shrimati Rajagopalan participated in the Hindustan Scouts 
Movement. She also took a leading part in the stude nts' movement 
during 1942 and attended training camp for relief w ork during the 
Second World War for the evacuees from Burma. Shrim ati 
Rajagopalan was a member of the Goodwill Mission to  Africa in the 
year 1965 and of the Indian Delegation to the Unite d Nations General 
Assembly. 
Shrimati Rajagopalan contributed short stories and articles in 
Tamil in various regional papers. 
Shrimati Rajagopalan represented the erstwhile Stat e of Madras, 
now Tamil Nadu, in Rajya Sabhafrom January, 1965 to April, 1970. 
32  

[22 November, 2006]           RAJYASABHA 
In the Passing away of Shrimati Rajgopalan the coun try has lost a 
noted social worker. 
Shri Ahmad Hossain Mondal passed away on the 8th Oc tober, 
2006, at the age of 79 years. He represented the St ate of West Bengal 
in this House from July, 1975 to July, 1981. 
Born at Bankra in the Howrah district of West Benga l in February, 
1928, Shri Mondal had his education at the Calcutta  University and 
Aligarh Muslim University. 
An advocate by profession, Shri Mondal was associat ed with 
various social welfare activities. He was Vice-Pres ident of the Indian 
Red Cross Society. 
The legislative career of Shri Mondal started with the membership 
of the West Bengal Legislative Council where he was  elected in the 
year 1964. Thereafter, he was elected to the West B engal Legislative 
Assembly in the 1967. 
A widely travelled person, Shri Mondal represented the country in 
the United Nations Coference on Trade and Developme nt at Nairobi, 
Kenya in the year 1976 and at International Red Cro ss Conference at 
Bucharest, Romania, in the year 1977. 
In the passing away of Shri Ahmad Hossain Mondal, t he country 
has lost a distinguished social worker and an able Parliamentarian. 
Shri Kanshi Ram passed away on the 9th October, 200 6, at the 
age of 73 years. He represented the State of Uttar Pradesh in this 
House from July 1998 to July 2004. He was leader of  the B.S.P. in the 
Rajya Sabha during this period. 
Born at Khawaspur village in the Ropar District of Punjab in 
March, 1934, Shri Kanshi Ram had his education at G overnment 
College, Ropar. 
Asocial worker, journalist and a writer, Shri Kansh i Ram was 
actively associated with the Dalit movement throughout the country 
and he mobilised them into a formidable political f orce in several 
States. He founded the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) in  the year 1984 
and remained its national President for almost two decades. 
33 

RAJYASABHA [22 November, 2006] 
 
The legislative career of Shri Kanshi Ram started w ith the 
membership of the Tenth Lok Sabha when he got elect ed in 1991. He 
was again elected to that House in the year 1996. 
In the passing away of Shri Kanshi Ram, the country  has lost a 
noted political personality, a dedicated social wor ker and a champion 
of Dalit movement. 
Shri Lalit Suri passed away on the 10th October, 20 06 at the age 
of 60 years following heart attack. He represented the State of Uttar 
Pradesh in this House for two terms from November, 2002 to July, 
2004 and July, 2004 till his untimely demise. 
Born at Rawalpindi, now in Pakistan, in April 1947,  Shri Suri had 
his education at Sri Ram College of Commerce, Delhi  University and 
Vauxhall Motors, U.K. 
An industrialist by profession, Shri Suri was also a dedicated 
social worker and involved in various charitable ac tivities for providing 
free facilities to pilgrims. 
A Diploma holder in Automobile Engineering, Shri Su ri switched 
over from automobiles to the hospitality business a nd rose to become 
one of the country's leading entrepreneurs in touri sm and hospitality 
sector. He established a network of hotels in vario us parts of the 
country and became the Chairman-cum-Managing Direct or of the 
Bharat Hotels Limited. He was also the President of  the Hotel 
Association of India. 
Shri Suri was instrumental in accelerating the pace  of growth of 
tourism industry in India. He was honoured by the G overnor of Jammu 
and Kashmir for promoting tourism in the State, des pite disturbed 
conditions there. He was also awarded World Travel Market Global 
Award, 2002, for promoting international cooperation through tou rism 
and National Tourism Award 2002-2003 from the Government of India 
for promoting tourism. Shri Suri was also the recip ient of several other 
prestigious awards namely, Hind Rattan, Udyog Rattan, Rajiv Gandhi 
Excellence Award and Excellence as Top CEO Award.  
A keen sports lover, Shri Suri was interested in golf, cricket and 
hockey. 
Shri Suri also brought out an afternoon newspaper n amed Delhi 
Midday.  
34 

[22 November, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
 
In the passing away of Shri Lalit Suri, the country  has lost a 
distinguished personality. 
Shri Santosh Kumar Sahu passed away on the 2nd Nove mber, 
2006, at the age of 71 years. 
Born at Baripada in the Mayurbhanj District of Oris sa in 
December, 1935, Shri Sahu had his education at M.P. C. College, 
Baripada; and Ravenshaw College and Madhusudan Law College, 
Cuttuck. 
An Advocate by profession, Shri Sahu was actively a ssociated 
with various social welfare and cultural organizati on. He took keen 
interest in the development of sports, co-operative s, economic 
planning and cultural activities. 
Shri Sahu was elected President of the Orissa State  co-operative 
Union in the years 1972,1977 and 1981. He also serv ed as President 
of the Orissa Sahitya Akademi, Orissa Sangeet Natak Akademi and 
Orissa Lalit KalaAkademi from 1963 to 1965; Orissa 
BlindmenAssociation, from 1976 to 1979; and Urban C o-operative 
Bank Institution, Bhubaneshwar, from 1988 to 1990. 
A keen sports lover, Shri Sahu served as President of the Orissa 
Cycling Association. He was also President of the A ll Orissa Volleyball 
Association from 1976 to 1981. 
Shri Sahu started his distinguished legislative car rer with the 
membership of Orissa Legislative Assembly. He also served as a 
Deputy Minister in the State Government of Orissa from 1962 to 1967. 
Shri Sahu represented the State of Orissa in this H ouse for three 
consecutive terms, from April, 1976 to April 1982, from April, 1982, to 
April 1988 and again from April, 1988 to April, 199 4. He was also 
nominated on the panel of Vice-Chairman, Rajya Sabh a during 1984 
to 1986. 
Shri Sahu attended the International Students' Conf erence held 
in Sri Lanka in 1956; Cultural Exchange Programme h eld in the 
U.S.A. in 1968 and Indo-Soviet Cultural Friendship Programme held 
in the U.S.S.R. in 1972. He was also a Member of th e Parliamentary 
Delegation to Zambia in 1980. 
In the passing away of Shri Santosh Kumar Sahu the country 
has lost a distinguished Parliamentarian. 
35 

RAJYASABHA [22 November, 2006] 
 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Sriman Pra fulla 
Goswami, Shrimati Lalitha Rajagopalan, Shri Ahmad H ossain Mondal, 
Shri Kanshi Ram, Shri Lalit Suri and Shri Santosh Kumar Sahu. 
I request hon. Members to rise in their seats and o bserve silence 
for one minute as a mark of respect to the departed soul. 
[Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute] 
MR, CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members 
of the bereaved families our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy. 
The House stands adjourned till 11.00 A.M. on Thursday, the 23rd 
November, 2006. 
The House then adjourned at seventeen minutes past eleven of the 
clock till eleven of the clock on Thursday, the 23rd November, 2006.

OBITUARY REFERENCE  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound Sorrow to the passing away of 
Shri Bhanu Pratap Singh, a former Member of this House on the 20th August, 2006, at the 
age of 90 years. 
Born in the Bulandshahr district of Uttar Pradesh in August 1917, Shri Singh had his 
education at Christian College, Lucknow, and Lucknow University Ar agriculturist by vocation, 
Shri Singh was associated with many social welfare and educational organisations in various 
capacities. He took  knee interesting in the promotion of education and setting up of hospitals. 
Shri Singh served as President of the Farmers' Federation of India. He was also Convener 
of the National Coordination Committee of Farm Organisations. 
Shri Singh edited many magazines concerning farmers. He also served as the editor of a 
journal named- Farmers Voice.' 
The legislative career of Shri Singh started with the membership of the Uttar Pradesh 
Legislative Assembly of which he was a member from 1962 to 196? and again from 1969 to 
1974. He represented the State of Uttar Pradesh in this House from April, 1976 to April, 
1982. 
Shri Singh had the distinction of serving as the Union Minister of State and help the 
portfolios of Agriculture, Irrigation and Rural Reconstruction. 
In the passing away of Shri Bhanu Pratap Singh, the country has lost a veteran 
parliamentarian, a distinguished social worker, an able administrator, and a true 
weil-wisher of the farming community. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Bhanu Pratap Singh.
